profile.name: Philip Stiber
profile.headline: Infrastructure & Security Leadership · Secure Enterprise Transformation · Controls & Resilience
profile.hook: When two companies become one, the technology has to merge — secure, audited, and running by Monday morning. Then comes the harder part: simplifying what was inherited, controlling it, and making it cheaper to run.
profile.summary: I lead the global infrastructure team at Tilray Brands, a multinational, regulated enterprise that grows by acquisition. My team integrates what the business acquires, retires what it no longer needs, and runs more than 50 of the SOX IT general controls it is audited on. I set direction, challenge designs and weigh cost against risk; experienced engineers own the plans, the delivery and the playbooks. CISSP- and CISM-certified, with more than fifteen years of hands-on depth behind the decisions.
profile.tagline: Engineer's judgement, leader's scope — infrastructure, security and business outcomes in one operating model.

rareStats.label: architecture and program, both validated
rareStats.note: CISSP covers security architecture and engineering; CISM covers running the security program and managing its risk. My work spans both, and so do the credentials.

rareStats.label: authorized to work in both countries
rareStats.note: Dual U.S. and Canadian citizenship: I can take a role or run an integration on either side of the border without visa or sponsorship friction.

rareStats.label: hands-on through leadership
rareStats.note: From desktop-to-server support to leading a distributed infrastructure team. The technical depth is what makes the challenge in design reviews credible.

rareStats.label: users, small office to global enterprise
rareStats.note: I've been the entire IT department for a small practice and led integration for a 900+-employee enterprise across two continents. The fundamentals scale; the operating model has to change.

rareStats.note: Infrastructure as code, detection engineering and automation built on my own time, kept separate from employer delivery.

profile.positioning: A technically grounded infrastructure leader who develops capable teams, directs secure enterprise transformation, and connects architecture, operational resilience and controls to measurable business value.

estate.intro: The brand portfolio behind the résumé. As Tilray Brands grew into a global beverage-alcohol and CPG enterprise, I led the infrastructure and M&A integration that brings each acquisition onto one secure, governed platform. Brands acquired 2023–2026.

transitions.text: Led the infrastructure and network integration for the acquisition of eight craft brands from Anheuser-Busch: system and network cutovers delivered on a 90-day clock.
Led the post-acquisition infrastructure transition for four craft brands acquired from Molson Coors: identity, email and network consolidated onto one governed platform.
Tilray acquired the BrewDog brand with its UK brewery and brewpubs, plus U.S. and Australian assets, in 2026.

experience.summary: Lead a distributed infrastructure team of 6–10 (a blend of full-time engineers and cloud consultants) supporting production facilities, brew pubs and offices across North America and Europe, inside an enterprise portfolio of 100+ active projects. Own the infrastructure SOX ITGC portfolio, direct acquisition-integration and cloud-consolidation strategy, spearhead IT's GMP compliance work, and help connect business continuity with technical recovery.

brief.headline: Integrated 10 acquisitions in 12 months, then turned to simplifying, controlling and reducing the cost of what was inherited.
brief.situation: A multinational, regulated enterprise growing by acquisition, inheriting overlapping networks, identities, clouds and platforms across 65+ sites in North America and Europe.
brief.action: Lead a 6–10-person team of engineers and cloud consultants who own migration plans, delivery and playbooks, while I set direction, challenge designs and prioritize through sprint planning. We integrated acquired organizations onto one governed identity and network platform and retired legacy estate. I run 50+ SOX ITGCs, lead IT's GMP compliance work, and am developing a phased consolidation strategy for an acquired multi-cloud environment.
brief.outcome: 10 organizations integrated in 12 months · 900+ employees on unified identity · 4 facilities taken over in 90 days · VM estate reduced by ~⅔ · six-figure annual OPEX reduction from legacy retirement · cloud consolidation underway, targeting a further six-figure annual OPEX reduction.

achievements.text: Led infrastructure integration for 10 acquired organizations within 12 months, including full system and network takeovers of 4 production facilities from AB InBev in 90 days and 6 Molson Coors transitions in 60 days, contributing to Tilray Beverages' growth into the #4 U.S. craft brewer.
achievements.impact: Each integration completed on schedule let the business consolidate operations sooner and reduce its dependence on sellers' transition services.

achievements.text: Built core security processes: phish-alert reporting, incident management, threat hunting, patching cycles, and coordinated incident response.
achievements.impact: Shifted the firm from reactive to proactive defense: faster detection and response shrink attacker dwell time and the financial and reputational cost of an incident — critical for a custodian of sensitive financial data.

problems.body: Compliance holds up when controls are part of how infrastructure runs day to day. I own a portfolio of 50+ SOX IT general controls and spearhead IT's GMP compliance work for international expansion.

problems.body: Business continuity and technical recovery are usually planned by different people. I bring business stakeholders into business impact analysis and sit in the small core group convened where the two intersect.

leadership.intro: The team I lead brings forward the plans, runs the migrations and improves the playbooks. My job is to keep that sustainable: set direction, add architectural judgement, and protect capacity for the improvements that make next quarter easier than this one.

I test designs against risk, cost, dependencies and alternatives.
The team executes. I contribute, and I take the significant escalations.

principles.t: Ownership stays with the people doing the work
principles.b: Engineers own plans, execution and playbooks. Continuity doesn't depend on any one person, including me.
Seniority means informed challenge and good trade-offs, not taking every hard ticket.

principles.t: Every delivery leaves a better playbook
principles.b: Repeatable beats remarkable. The tenth migration should be easier than the first.
Simplification competes with a large portfolio. I make the case for it inside real operational constraints.

caseStudies.title: Integrating acquisitions onto one governed platform
caseStudies.summary: Ten acquired organizations brought onto one governed identity and network platform in twelve months.
caseStudies.problem: A run of acquisitions, including craft-brewing businesses acquired from Anheuser-Busch and Molson Coors, each arrived with its own identity tenant, email, network and support arrangements. The production sites had to keep running throughout.
caseStudies.constraints: Transition-service deadlines, live production facilities, public-company controls, and a lean team spread across two continents.
caseStudies.role: Led the infrastructure integration plan and sequencing, set the target state, and coordinated cutovers with the sellers' teams and the business.
caseStudies.team: Engineers planned and executed the tenant, email, Meraki and Active Directory migrations and the facility cutovers.
decisions: One governed target (Entra ID / Microsoft 365) for every acquisition, so each integration followed a repeatable path.
Exit transition-service dependencies on the seller early.
Plan facility takeovers around protecting production continuity through the ownership transfer.
caseStudies.outcome: 10 organizations integrated within 12 months. Four production facilities taken over in 90 days, six Molson Coors migrations completed in 60 days, and six Entra tenant-to-tenant migrations that moved 900+ employees onto unified identity.

caseStudies.title: Rationalizing a legacy estate
caseStudies.summary: Deliberate selection and retirement shrank the virtual-machine estate to about a third of its size and cut annual OPEX.
caseStudies.problem: Years of acquisitions left overlapping platforms and a large virtual-machine estate: more to secure, patch, license and support than the business needed.
caseStudies.constraints: Systems still in use by production and corporate teams, application owners with competing priorities, and change capacity shared with a large project portfolio.
caseStudies.role: Built the case for retirement, chose what to keep and what to sunset, and secured leadership support for the program.
caseStudies.team: Engineers validated dependencies, migrated the remaining workloads and decommissioned platforms.
decisions: Deliberate selection over blanket lift-and-shift: retire first, and migrate only what earns its place.
Treat each retirement as a cost, risk and support decision, not only a technical one.
caseStudies.outcome: The virtual-machine estate is now roughly one-third of its earlier size. Separately, retiring legacy platforms delivered a six-figure reduction in annual operating expense, and further opportunities have been identified.

caseStudies.title: Consolidating an acquired cloud environment
caseStudies.summary: A phased strategy to move an acquired multi-cloud estate into an enduring landing zone.
caseStudies.problem: An acquired business runs a multi-cloud (Azure and AWS) environment with a substantial annual run rate and network dependencies of its own.
caseStudies.constraints: Live applications, including ecommerce integrations; BGP and network dependencies; and the need to land workloads in an environment that will still make sense in five years.
caseStudies.role: Developed the phased migration and consolidation strategy and defined the target operating environment.
caseStudies.team: Engineers plan and execute the phases, including AWS-to-Azure application-stack moves and BGP cutovers.
decisions: Land workloads in the governed Azure landing zones established through the CAF program, rather than migrating into a temporary state.
Move in phases, with cutovers sequenced around network and application dependencies.
Judge success by the reduction in run rate, not by the number of workloads moved.
caseStudies.outcome: Underway. The strategy targets a substantial six-figure reduction in annual operating expense. That figure is an estimate and has not yet been realized.

caseStudies.title: Bringing regulated systems under GMP control
caseStudies.summary: System validation, ITGCs and recovery attestations for a business unit entering GMP-regulated markets.
caseStudies.problem: A business unit expanding into international markets has to meet Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP) expectations for the computerized systems its laboratory and production processes depend on.
caseStudies.constraints: Lab equipment and lab software are in scope, and so is the ERP at one facility. Validation has to fit around live operations, and recovery commitments must be attested, not assumed.
caseStudies.role: Spearhead IT's GMP compliance work: scoping, system validation, ITGCs and RPO/RTO attestations for in-scope systems.
caseStudies.team: The infrastructure team supports the infrastructure and operations around the in-scope ERP.
decisions: Scope explicitly: lab equipment, lab software and one facility's ERP, not the whole estate.
Attest recovery point and recovery time objectives (RPO/RTO) for in-scope systems instead of assuming them.
Build on the existing ITGC discipline rather than creating a parallel control set.
caseStudies.outcome: In progress. This is readiness work; no certification or regulatory approval is claimed.

caseStudies.title: Connecting business impact to technical recovery
caseStudies.summary: Business impact analysis as the common starting point for continuity and disaster recovery.
caseStudies.problem: Continuity plans and disaster-recovery plans often describe the same systems in different terms, and different people own them.
caseStudies.constraints: Accountability shared across business and IT leadership, and recovery priorities that have to reflect how the business actually makes and ships its products.
caseStudies.role: Brought business stakeholders together to run business impact analyses. I'm a member of the small core leadership group called on where business continuity and technical recovery intersect.
caseStudies.team: The infrastructure team maps technical dependencies and supports recovery planning.
decisions: Start from business impact, not from the server list.
Frame infrastructure and production-environment risk with NIST SP 800-53 and SP 800-82 to measure progress and prioritize investment.
caseStudies.outcome: Ongoing. Business impact analyses give continuity and recovery planning a shared, business-first starting point.

caseStudies.title: Repeatable cloud delivery as code
caseStudies.summary: My team owns the infrastructure as code; Azure Virtual Desktop is being delivered from Bicep templates.
caseStudies.problem: Virtual desktop platforms built by hand are hard to reproduce, review and audit.
caseStudies.constraints: Enterprise change control, identity and network integration, and four disciplines contributing to the same templates.
caseStudies.role: I run the team that owns and controls the infrastructure as code.
caseStudies.team: A joint effort across infrastructure, network engineering, information security and cloud architecture. Artifacts are versioned in the enterprise repository.
decisions: Declarative templates instead of portal builds, so the environment can be reviewed, reproduced and audited.
Keep artifacts in the enterprise repository so the design outlives any one engineer.
caseStudies.outcome: Deployment is in progress. It is a current example of the team's infrastructure-as-code practice.
